units.title: Make first contact
units.description: Greet, exchange names, and choose familiar or polite address.

lessons.title: Begin and end an exchange
lessons.outcome: I can greet someone and take leave.

targets.label: Begin and end an exchange
targets.explanation: Ciao is familiar; buongiorno is a polite greeting; arrivederci ends an exchange.

repair.title: Try begin and end an exchange again
repair.body: Ciao can greet or say goodbye to a friend. Buongiorno opens a polite daytime exchange. Arrivederci closes an exchange politely.

examples.it: Ciao, Anna!
examples.en: Hi, Anna!

examples.it: Buongiorno, signora.
examples.en: Good day, madam.

examples.it: Grazie, signora. Arrivederci!
examples.en: Thank you, madam. Goodbye!

familiar-greeting.title: Greet a friend
familiar-greeting.body: When a familiar friend arrives, ciao is a natural greeting.

examples.it: Ciao, Sara!
examples.en: Hi, Sara!

polite-greeting.title: Open a polite daytime exchange
polite-greeting.body: Use buongiorno when beginning this polite daytime exchange. Arrivederci is for leaving.

examples.it: Buongiorno, dottore.
examples.en: Good day, doctor.

farewell.title: End the exchange
farewell.body: Arrivederci is a polite goodbye. The person is leaving, so this is a farewell rather than an arrival greeting.

examples.it: Grazie, signora. Arrivederci!
examples.en: Thank you, madam. Goodbye!

lessons.title: Exchange names
lessons.outcome: I can ask and give a name with a model.

targets.label: Exchange names
targets.explanation: Mi chiamo… and Come ti chiami? are useful whole phrases; their verb parts are explained later.

repair.title: Try exchange names again
repair.body: Say Mi chiamo followed by a name. Keep the whole expression together.

examples.it: Mi chiamo Anna.
examples.en: My name is Anna.

lessons.title: Ask a name politely
lessons.outcome: I can choose a polite name question for a stranger.

targets.label: Ask a name politely
targets.explanation: Come si chiama? is the polite whole question; Come ti chiami? is familiar. Do not infer the full reflexive pattern yet.

repair.title: Try ask a name politely again
repair.body: Use Come ti chiami? with a peer you call tu. Use Come si chiama? for polite Lei address.

examples.it: Buongiorno, signora. Come si chiama?
examples.en: Good morning, madam. What is your name?

units.title: Keep the exchange going
units.description: Use courtesy and repair phrases in short conversations.

lessons.title: Thank and ask politely
lessons.outcome: I can use grazie, prego, scusi and per favore in their different jobs.

targets.label: Thank and ask politely
targets.explanation: Grazie thanks someone; prego responds; scusi gets attention; per favore softens a request.

repair.title: Try thank and ask politely again
repair.body: Grazie thanks someone. Prego is a natural answer to thanks.

examples.it: «Grazie!» «Prego!»
examples.en: “Thank you!” “You are welcome!”

lessons.title: Ask for a repeat
lessons.outcome: I can say I do not understand and ask for repetition.

targets.label: Ask for a repeat
targets.explanation: Non capisco and Può ripetere, per favore? are whole repair expressions. Their internal grammar comes later.

repair.title: Try ask for a repeat again
repair.body: Use Non capisco when you have not understood.

examples.it: Scusi, non capisco.
examples.en: Excuse me, I do not understand.

units.title: Connect meaning and sound
units.description: Use supported origin phrases and hear familiar spelling patterns.

lessons.title: Say where you are from
lessons.outcome: I can use Sono di with a supplied place name.

targets.label: Say where you are from
targets.explanation: Sono di Roma means I am from Rome. Keep sono di as a whole origin frame for now.

repair.title: Try say where you are from again
repair.body: Say Sono di plus the supplied city name. You do not need a general preposition rule yet.

examples.it: Sono di Roma.
examples.en: I am from Rome.

lessons.title: Read two c patterns
lessons.outcome: I can connect familiar c spellings with their taught sounds.

targets.label: Read two c patterns
targets.explanation: C before a or o is hard in casa and come. C before e is soft in cena. In ciao the i signals soft c but is not a separate vowel sound.

repair.title: Try hear two c sounds again
repair.body: In casa and come, c before a or o has a hard sound. Listen to both known words.

examples.it: La casa è a Roma.
examples.en: The house is in Rome.

lessons.title: Keep c hard before e and i
lessons.outcome: I can recognize ch in a few introduced words.

targets.label: Recognize ch before e and i
targets.explanation: Ch keeps c hard before e or i in these familiar words.

repair.title: Notice the h
repair.body: Compare soft c in cena with hard ch in che. The h changes the spelling pattern, not the meaning of an unknown sentence.

examples.it: che · chi · il chilo
examples.en: what/that · who · the kilo

units.title: Say who you are
units.description: Turn familiar identity phrases into reusable essere forms.

lessons.title: Use sono, sei and è
lessons.outcome: I can choose essere for I, familiar you, and one other person.

targets.label: Use sono, sei and è
targets.explanation: Io sono, tu sei, and Anna è identify three different people. The pronoun may be omitted when the form is clear.

repair.title: Try use sono, sei and è again
repair.body: Use sono with io, sei with tu, and è with one named person. Sono, sei and è are present forms of essere.

examples.it: Io sono Anna. Tu sei Luca.
examples.en: I am Anna. You are Luca.

lessons.title: Use Lei è politely
lessons.outcome: I can ask or tell who a person is using polite Lei.

targets.label: Use Lei è politely
targets.explanation: Lei addresses one person politely but takes the same verb form è as one other person. The social relationship controls the choice.

repair.title: Try use lei è politely again
repair.body: When you address one person as Lei, use è, not sei. Use tu sei with a familiar peer.

examples.it: Signora, Lei è di Firenze?
examples.en: Madam, are you from Florence?

lessons.title: Introduce two or more people
lessons.outcome: I can use siamo, siete and sono with plural people.

targets.label: Introduce two or more people
targets.explanation: Noi siamo, voi siete, loro sono are plural forms of essere. The verb says who is meant even without the pronoun.

repair.title: Try introduce two or more people again
repair.body: Use siamo for we, siete for you all, and sono for they. These are all forms of essere.

examples.it: Noi siamo di Milano. Voi siete di Roma.
examples.en: We are from Milan. You all are from Rome.

lessons.title: Give vowels and stress their place
lessons.outcome: I can recognize familiar vowel spellings and marked final stress.

targets.label: I can recognize familiar vowel spellings and marked final stress.
targets.explanation: Learn the sound with the word. Final written accents in città and caffè mark a stressed final vowel.

repair.title: Compare the familiar words
repair.body: Italian has five vowel letters: a, e, i, o, u. Keep vowel sounds clear when you imitate the examples. E and o each have open and closed pronunciations; spelling alone does not always tell you which. Many familiar words stress the second-to-last syllable, as in casa, but this is not a rule for every word. A written final accent marks final stress: città, caffè.

examples.it: La casa è a Roma.
examples.en: The house is in Rome.

examples.it: Un caffè in città.
examples.en: A coffee in town.

lessons.title: Keep the written accent
lessons.outcome: I can distinguish e from è and preserve familiar final accents.

targets.label: I can distinguish e from è and preserve familiar final accents.
targets.explanation: Use e for and and è for is. Accents are part of the spelling, including città, caffè and perché.

repair.title: Compare the familiar words
repair.body: È means is; e means and. The written accent changes the word. Keep the final accents in città and caffè. Perché ends with an acute é; caffè ends with a grave è. Learn these spellings with each word.

examples.it: Anna e Luca. Anna è qui.
examples.en: Anna and Luca. Anna is here.

examples.it: Un caffè in città.
examples.en: A coffee in town.

units.title: Name familiar things
units.description: Learn noun gender and singular articles with known objects and people.

lessons.title: Name a familiar noun
lessons.outcome: I can use il or la with familiar singular nouns.

targets.label: Name a familiar noun
targets.explanation: Learn a noun with its article: il libro and il pane are masculine; la casa and la scuola are feminine. Endings help, but -e does not settle gender.

repair.title: Try name a familiar noun again
repair.body: Il introduces these masculine nouns; la introduces these feminine nouns. The article is part of the form you learn.

examples.it: Il libro è qui. La casa è qui.
examples.en: The book is here. The house is here.

lessons.title: Introduce one thing
lessons.outcome: I can distinguish un, una and un’ with a familiar noun.

targets.label: Introduce one thing
targets.explanation: Use un with a masculine noun, una with a feminine consonant, and un’ before a feminine vowel. The apostrophe joins directly to the noun.

repair.title: Try introduce one thing again
repair.body: Use un with masculine nouns, including un amico without an apostrophe. Use una before a feminine consonant. Before a feminine vowel, una becomes un’ and joins the noun: un’amica.

examples.it: È un libro. È una casa.
examples.en: It is a book. It is a house.

examples.it: Luca è un amico. Anna è un’amica.
examples.en: Luca is a male friend. Anna is a female friend.

masculine-un.title: One masculine noun
masculine-un.body: Masculine nouns take un here. There is no apostrophe even before the vowel of amico.

examples.it: Un libro. Un amico.
examples.en: A book. A male friend.

feminine-una.title: One feminine noun before a consonant
feminine-una.body: Casa is feminine and begins with a consonant, so keep una.

examples.it: È una casa.
examples.en: It is a house.

feminine-elision.title: Join un’ to a feminine vowel
feminine-elision.body: Amica is feminine and starts with a vowel. Una loses its final a: un’amica. Join the apostrophe directly to the noun. Masculine un amico has no apostrophe.

examples.it: Sara è un’amica. Luca è un amico.
examples.en: Sara is a female friend. Luca is a male friend.

lessons.title: Name a student or a backpack
lessons.outcome: I can use lo/uno and l’ with their taught nouns.

targets.label: Name a student or a backpack
targets.explanation: Use lo and uno before masculine z or s plus another consonant; use l’ before a singular vowel noun. Keep gender separate from the opening sound.

repair.title: Try name a student or a backpack again
repair.body: Lo studente and lo zaino are definite. For one new student or backpack, use uno.

examples.it: Lo zaino è qui. È uno zaino.
examples.en: The backpack is here. It is a backpack.

units.title: Say what you have
units.description: Use avere for possessions, ages, and basic physical states.

lessons.title: Say what one person has
lessons.outcome: I can use ho, hai and ha for possessions.

targets.label: Say what one person has
targets.explanation: Io ho, tu hai, and Anna ha come from avere. The written h is silent but distinguishes these forms.

repair.title: Try say what one person has again
repair.body: Use ho for I, hai for familiar you, and ha for one other person.

examples.it: Io ho un libro. Tu hai uno zaino.
examples.en: I have a book. You have a backpack.

lessons.title: Say what a group has
lessons.outcome: I can choose abbiamo, avete and hanno.

targets.label: Say what a group has
targets.explanation: Noi abbiamo, voi avete, and loro hanno are the plural present forms of avere. Hanno has silent h.

repair.title: Try say what a group has again
repair.body: Use abbiamo for we, avete for you all, and hanno for they.

examples.it: Noi abbiamo un libro. Voi avete uno zaino.
examples.en: We have a book. You all have a backpack.

lessons.title: Read small numbers
lessons.outcome: I can recognize and say zero through ten in practical information.

targets.label: Read small numbers
targets.explanation: Learn number words in small groups, then connect the spoken word to a digit. Age and prices use this knowledge later.

repair.title: Try read small numbers again
repair.body: Listen to zero, uno, due, tre, quattro and cinque. Match each to its digit.

examples.it: Il numero è due.
examples.en: The number is two.

lessons.title: Give an age and a need
lessons.outcome: I can use avere to state a modeled age or hunger and thirst.

targets.label: Give an age and a need
targets.explanation: Italian uses avere in ho otto anni, ho fame and ho sete. Use fictional people for age practice; larger numbers come later.

repair.title: Try give an age and a need again
repair.body: Say ho otto anni for “I am eight years old.” The age here belongs to a fictional child.

examples.it: Luca ha otto anni. Anna ha nove anni.
examples.en: Luca is eight. Anna is nine.

lessons.title: Write h without sounding it
lessons.outcome: I can keep the silent h in familiar avere forms.

targets.label: I can keep the silent h in familiar avere forms.
targets.explanation: Silent does not mean optional: keep h in these avere forms. The word o means or.

repair.title: Compare the familiar words
repair.body: The h in ho, hai, ha and hanno is silent. It still belongs in their spelling. Ho means I have; o means or. They can sound alike, so use the meaning and the sentence, not an extra h sound, to choose.

examples.it: Ho un libro. Tè o caffè?
examples.en: I have a book. Tea or coffee?

examples.it: Anna ha uno zaino.
examples.en: Anna has a backpack.

units.title: Describe one or several things
units.description: Build regular plurals, plural articles and simple adjective agreement.

lessons.title: Make familiar nouns plural
lessons.outcome: I can form regular plurals of taught nouns.

targets.label: Make familiar nouns plural
targets.explanation: Libro → libri, casa → case, studente → studenti. A noun ending alone does not say which article to use.

repair.title: Try make familiar nouns plural again
repair.body: A regular -o noun changes to -i; a regular -a noun changes to -e.

examples.it: Un libro, due libri. Una casa, due case.
examples.en: One book, two books. One house, two houses.

lessons.title: Put an article before a plural
lessons.outcome: I can choose i, gli and le for taught plurals.

targets.label: Put an article before a plural
targets.explanation: Il libro → i libri; lo studente → gli studenti; la casa → le case. Learn the plural article after the noun plural.

repair.title: Try put an article before a plural again
repair.body: Il becomes i before a regular masculine plural; la becomes le before a feminine plural.

examples.it: I libri sono qui. Le case sono qui.
examples.en: The books are here. The houses are here.

lessons.title: Keep a hard sound in the plural
lessons.outcome: I can write amiche and know that città does not change.

targets.label: Keep a hard sound in the plural
targets.explanation: Amica → amiche keeps hard c before e with h. Città is invariant: one city, two città; the article or number shows plural.

repair.title: Try keep a hard sound in the plural again
repair.body: Amica becomes amiche. The h keeps the hard c sound before e.

examples.it: Un’amica, due amiche.
examples.en: One female friend, two female friends.

lessons.title: Match a basic description
lessons.outcome: I can match piccolo or grande to a familiar noun.

targets.label: Match a basic description
targets.explanation: Piccolo changes for gender and number: piccolo, piccola, piccoli, piccole. Grande is singular for both genders; grandi is plural.

repair.title: Try match a basic description again
repair.body: A four-form adjective agrees with its noun: il libro piccolo, la casa piccola, i libri piccoli, le case piccole.

examples.it: La casa è piccola. I libri sono piccoli.
examples.en: The house is small. The books are small.

lessons.title: Give double consonants time
lessons.outcome: I can preserve a familiar single/double-consonant spelling contrast.

targets.label: I can preserve a familiar single/double-consonant spelling contrast.
targets.explanation: Consonant length can distinguish words. Do not drop the double l in palla or double n in penna.

repair.title: Compare the familiar words
repair.body: A double consonant is held longer. Pala and palla are different words; so are pena and penna. Listen to the whole word, keep the vowel clear, and give the written double consonant its extra time. Meaning also helps you choose the spelling.

examples.it: La pala. La palla.
examples.en: The shovel. The ball.

examples.it: La pena. La penna.
examples.en: The sorrow or penalty. The pen.

units.title: Talk about everyday actions
units.description: Use -are verbs, questions and negation for familiar routines.

lessons.title: Say who speaks or lives somewhere
lessons.outcome: I can use regular -are verbs with I, you, and one other person.

targets.label: Say who speaks or lives somewhere
targets.explanation: For parlare, use parlo, parli, parla. Abitare follows the same endings: abito, abiti, abita. Polite Lei uses the same form as one other person.

repair.title: Try say who speaks or lives somewhere again
repair.body: Remove -are, then use -o for io, -i for tu, and -a for lui/lei or polite Lei.

examples.it: Io parlo italiano. Tu parli italiano.
examples.en: I speak Italian. You speak Italian.

lessons.title: Talk about a group action
lessons.outcome: I can use -iamo, -ate and -ano for regular -are verbs.

targets.label: Talk about a group action
targets.explanation: Parliamo is we speak, parlate is you all speak, and parlano is they speak. Other regular -are verbs reuse these endings.

repair.title: Try talk about a group action again
repair.body: For parlare, remove -are and add -iamo, -ate, or -ano for noi, voi, and loro.

examples.it: Noi parliamo. Voi parlate. Loro parlano.
examples.en: We speak. You all speak. They speak.

lessons.title: Ask a simple question
lessons.outcome: I can ask a yes/no or dove question using a taught present form.

targets.label: Ask a simple question
targets.explanation: A yes/no question can keep statement word order and use a question mark and voice contour. Dove asks where; the verb still agrees with its person.

repair.title: Try ask a simple question again
repair.body: Keep the taught verb form and raise the question in speech or writing.

examples.it: Tu abiti a Roma?
examples.en: Do you live in Rome?

lessons.title: Say what does not happen
lessons.outcome: I can put non before a known present verb.

targets.label: Say what does not happen
targets.explanation: Put non immediately before the conjugated verb: non parlo, non mangiamo. It does not change the verb ending.

repair.title: Try say what does not happen again
repair.body: Place non before the conjugated present verb.

examples.it: Non parlo italiano.
examples.en: I do not speak Italian.

lessons.title: Turn a statement into a question
lessons.outcome: I can recognize a familiar question and practise its intonation.

targets.label: I can recognize a familiar question and practise its intonation.
targets.explanation: A yes/no question does not need English do. Word order may stay the same; punctuation and voice show the question.

repair.title: Compare the familiar words
repair.body: A simple yes/no question can keep the same word order as a statement. In writing, the question mark shows that an answer is expected: Parli italiano? In speech, use an appropriate question contour; many neutral yes/no questions rise near the end, but Italian intonation varies by context and region.

examples.it: Parli italiano. Parli italiano?
examples.en: You speak Italian. Do you speak Italian?

examples.it: Abiti a Roma. Abiti a Roma?
examples.en: You live in Rome. Do you live in Rome?

units.title: Expand everyday actions
units.description: Use regular -ere, -ire and -isc present patterns with useful routines.

lessons.title: Use vivere and prendere
lessons.outcome: I can choose present -ere forms for familiar persons.

targets.label: Use vivere and prendere
targets.explanation: Vivere gives vivo, vivi, vive, viviamo, vivete, vivono. Prendere follows the same person endings with its own stem.

repair.title: Try use vivere and prendere again
repair.body: Vivere: io vivo, tu vivi, lui/lei/Lei vive, noi viviamo, voi vivete, loro vivono. Prendere: io prendo, tu prendi, lui/lei/Lei prende, noi prendiamo, voi prendete, loro prendono. Formal Lei uses the singular third-person form.

examples.it: Voi vivete a Roma. Anna e Luca prendono il treno.
examples.en: You all live in Rome. Anna and Luca take the train.

lessons.title: Use dormire and partire
lessons.outcome: I can use ordinary -ire endings with a known verb.

targets.label: Use dormire and partire
targets.explanation: Dormire gives dormo, dormi, dorme, dormiamo, dormite, dormono. Partire follows the same pattern in these forms.

repair.title: Try use dormire and partire again
repair.body: Dormire: io dormo, tu dormi, lui/lei/Lei dorme, noi dormiamo, voi dormite, loro dormono. Partire: io parto, tu parti, lui/lei/Lei parte, noi partiamo, voi partite, loro partono. These verbs do not add -isc-. Formal Lei takes dorme or parte.

examples.it: Noi dormiamo a casa. Anna e Luca partono domani.
examples.en: We sleep at home. Anna and Luca leave tomorrow.

lessons.title: Use capire
lessons.outcome: I can use the taught -isc- forms of capire.

targets.label: Use capire
targets.explanation: Capire has capisco, capisci, capisce, capiamo, capite, capiscono. The -isc- part is absent in noi and voi.

repair.title: Try use capire again
repair.body: Capire adds -isc- in io, tu, lui/lei and loro, but not in noi and voi.

examples.it: Io capisco. Tu capisci. Anna capisce.
examples.en: I understand. You understand. Anna understands.

lessons.title: Read g and gh in familiar words
lessons.outcome: I can recognize the taught hard and soft g patterns.

targets.label: I can recognize the taught hard and soft g patterns.
targets.explanation: Compare soft g in gelato and giro with hard g in gatto, spaghetti and ghiaccio.

repair.title: Compare the familiar words
repair.body: G before a, o or u is normally hard, as in gatto. Before e or i it is normally soft, as in gelato and giro. Gh keeps the sound hard before e or i: spaghetti and ghiaccio. In ghiaccio, the first i is heard as a brief glide, like y in yes; h stays silent.

examples.it: Il gatto. Il gelato.
examples.en: The cat. The ice cream.

examples.it: Gli spaghetti. Il ghiaccio.
examples.en: Spaghetti. Ice.

units.title: Go places and do things
units.description: Use selected irregular presents and basic place relationships.

lessons.title: Say where you go
lessons.outcome: I can use selected present forms of andare in a plan.

targets.label: Say where you go
targets.explanation: Andare is irregular: vado, vai, va, andiamo. Use the form that fits the traveler.

repair.title: Try say where you go again
repair.body: Andare: io vado, tu vai, lui/lei/Lei va, noi andiamo, voi andate, loro vanno. Formal Lei uses va when addressing one person politely.

examples.it: Voi andate a Milano domani? Loro vanno a Roma.
examples.en: Are you all going to Milan tomorrow? They go to Rome.

lessons.title: Say what you do or make
lessons.outcome: I can use selected forms of fare in familiar activities.

targets.label: Say what you do or make
targets.explanation: Fare is irregular: faccio, fai, fa, facciamo. Learn these common forms with their person.

repair.title: Try say what you do or make again
repair.body: Fare: io faccio, tu fai, lui/lei/Lei fa, noi facciamo, voi fate, loro fanno. Formal Lei uses fa when addressing one person politely.

examples.it: Voi fate colazione a casa? Anna e Luca fanno una torta.
examples.en: Do you all have breakfast at home? Anna and Luca make a cake.

lessons.title: Say who comes
lessons.outcome: I can use selected present forms of venire.

targets.label: Say who comes
targets.explanation: Venire has vengo, vieni, viene, veniamo in these familiar persons. With origin, use da: vengo da Roma.

repair.title: Try say who comes again
repair.body: Venire: io vengo, tu vieni, lui/lei/Lei viene, noi veniamo, voi venite, loro vengono. Formal Lei uses viene when addressing one person politely.

examples.it: Voi venite da Napoli? Anna e Luca vengono da Roma.
examples.en: Do you all come from Naples? Anna and Luca come from Rome.

lessons.title: Go to a city or country
lessons.outcome: I can use a with taught cities and in with taught countries.

targets.label: Go to a city or country
targets.explanation: Use a with a city: a Roma. Use in with a country: in Italia. Learn destination phrases with the place name.

repair.title: Try go to a city or country again
repair.body: Use a before these city names when saying where someone goes.

examples.it: Vado a Roma. Andiamo a Milano.
examples.en: I go to Rome. We go to Milan.

lessons.title: Come from and go with
lessons.outcome: I can use da for source and con for a companion.

targets.label: Come from and go with
targets.explanation: Vengo da Roma gives a source; vado con Luca names a companion. These answer different questions.

repair.title: Try come from and go with again
repair.body: Da tells where someone comes from in vengo da + city.

examples.it: Vengo da Napoli.
examples.en: I come from Naples.

lessons.title: Read sc and sch
lessons.outcome: I can recognize the taught soft sc and hard sc/sch patterns.

targets.label: I can recognize the taught soft sc and hard sc/sch patterns.
targets.explanation: Scena and pesce use soft sc. Scuola and schermo have the hard sound; h preserves it before e.

repair.title: Compare the familiar words
repair.body: Sc before e or i has the soft sound heard in scena and pesce. Sc before a, o or u is hard, as in scuola. Sch keeps that hard sound before e or i, as in schermo. Listen to the known word before practising its spelling.

examples.it: La scena. Il pesce.
examples.en: The scene. The fish.

examples.it: La scuola. Lo schermo.
examples.en: The school. The screen.

units.title: Find things and places
units.description: Express what is present and locate familiar people or objects.

lessons.title: Say what is there
lessons.outcome: I can choose c’è or ci sono for one or several things.

targets.label: Say what is there
targets.explanation: C’è goes with one count noun or a mass noun; ci sono goes with plurals. These phrases also keep their form in questions.

repair.title: Try say what is there again
repair.body: Use c’è before one count noun or an uncountable amount.

examples.it: C’è una stazione qui. C’è acqua.
examples.en: There is a station here. There is water.

lessons.title: Say where a place is
lessons.outcome: I can say a familiar thing is near or far from a known place.

targets.label: Say where a place is
targets.explanation: Vicino a means near; lontano da means far from. As adjectives, vicino/vicina and lontano/lontana agree with the thing located.

repair.title: Try say where a place is again
repair.body: Vicino a means near and lontano da means far from. The adjective may agree with the thing located; the invariant location phrases are also valid in these sentences.

examples.it: La casa è vicina a Roma / vicino a Roma.
examples.en: The house is near Rome: both forms are valid.

examples.it: La scuola è lontana da Milano / lontano da Milano.
examples.en: The school is far from Milan: both forms are valid.

near.title: Keep the near meaning
near.body: Vicina a is the agreeing adjective with a feminine noun. The invariant phrase vicino a is also valid here. Both mean near; lontano da means far from.

examples.it: La casa è vicino a Roma.
examples.en: The house is near Rome.

far.title: Keep the far-from meaning
far.body: Lontana da is the agreeing adjective with a feminine noun. The invariant phrase lontano da is also valid here. Both mean far from; vicino a means near.

examples.it: La scuola è lontano da Milano.
examples.en: The school is far from Milan.

lessons.title: Join a or in to an article
lessons.outcome: I can use al/alla and nel/nella with familiar places.

targets.label: Join a or in to an article
targets.explanation: A + il/la gives al/alla; in + il/la gives nel/nella. Choose the place meaning first, then its article.

repair.title: Try join a or in to an article again
repair.body: Use al for a + il and alla for a + la.

examples.it: Vado al mercato. Vado alla stazione.
examples.en: I go to the market. I go to the station.

units.title: Say whose and which
units.description: Identify possessions and choose nearby or more distant things.

lessons.title: Say something is mine
lessons.outcome: I can match mio/mia/miei/mie to a known noun.

targets.label: Say something is mine
targets.explanation: The thing owned determines the form: il mio libro, la mia casa, i miei libri, le mie case.

repair.title: Try say something is mine again
repair.body: Use il mio with libro and la mia with casa.

examples.it: Il mio libro è qui. La mia casa è vicina.
examples.en: My book is here. My house is nearby.

lessons.title: Talk about your family
lessons.outcome: I can say mia madre and tuo padre without an article.

targets.label: Talk about your family
targets.explanation: With one close family member, normally omit the article: mia madre, tuo padre. Keep the article with an ordinary noun: il mio amico.

repair.title: Try talk about your family again
repair.body: Say mia madre and tuo padre, without an article, for one close family member.

examples.it: Mia madre è qui. Tuo padre è a Roma.
examples.en: My mother is here. Your father is in Rome.

lessons.title: Point to this or that
lessons.outcome: I can select questo/questa and quel/quella for familiar things.

targets.label: Point to this or that
targets.explanation: Questo/questa point to something near. Quel/quella identify something farther away or already mentioned; match gender.

repair.title: Try point to this or that again
repair.body: Use questo libro and questa casa for things near you.

examples.it: Questo libro è piccolo. Questa casa è grande.
examples.en: This book is small. This house is big.

lessons.title: Read gn and gli as groups
lessons.outcome: I can recognize gn and gli in introduced everyday words.

targets.label: I can recognize gn and gli in introduced everyday words.
targets.explanation: Learn gn in bagno and gnocchi, and gli in famiglia and figlio, as joined sound patterns.

repair.title: Compare the familiar words
repair.body: In bagno and gnocchi, gn represents one joined sound rather than a separate g and n. In famiglia and figlio, gli likewise makes a joined sound. These are useful familiar patterns, not a rule for every spelling beginning gli: for example glicine (wisteria) is different. Imitate the words as units.

examples.it: Il bagno. Gli gnocchi.
examples.en: The bathroom. Gnocchi.

examples.it: La famiglia. Il figlio.
examples.en: The family. The son.

units.title: Buy and arrange things
units.description: Use introduced numbers, prices, times and amounts in a short transaction.

lessons.title: Recognize eleven through twenty
lessons.outcome: I can read and use selected numbers from eleven to twenty.

targets.label: Recognize eleven through twenty
targets.explanation: Learn undici through venti in two small groups, then retrieve the words in practical counts.

repair.title: Try recognize eleven through twenty again
repair.body: Hear and read undici, dodici, tredici, quattordici and quindici.

examples.it: Il numero è dodici.
examples.en: The number is twelve.

lessons.title: Ask and understand a price
lessons.outcome: I can use introduced tens in a simple euro price.

targets.label: Ask and understand a price
targets.explanation: Learn trenta, quaranta, cinquanta and cento as price words before using them; quanto costa? asks a price.

repair.title: Try ask and understand a price again
repair.body: Quanto costa? is a useful whole question about one item. Prices use numbers you have learned.

examples.it: Quanto costa il libro? Costa trenta euro.
examples.en: How much is the book? It costs thirty euros.

lessons.title: Make a simple appointment
lessons.outcome: I can use a taught day and alle/all’una with a clock time.

targets.label: Make a simple appointment
targets.explanation: Say alle otto, alle nove, but all’una. Use a named day to place a routine event.

repair.title: Try make a simple appointment again
repair.body: Use alle before most stated clock hours: alle otto, alle nove.

examples.it: Il treno parte lunedì alle otto.
examples.en: The train leaves Monday at eight.

lessons.title: Say many or few
lessons.outcome: I can match molto/poco to familiar count and mass nouns.

targets.label: Say many or few
targets.explanation: With count nouns, molto/poco agree: molti libri, poche case. With water, use singular molta acqua or poca acqua.

repair.title: Try say many or few again
repair.body: Use plural forms with counted nouns: molti libri, poche case.

examples.it: Ho molti libri. Anna ha poche case.
examples.en: I have many books. Anna has few houses.

units.title: Ask, respond and express preferences
units.description: Make familiar requests, say what you want, and give a brief reason.

lessons.title: Ask if you can do something
lessons.outcome: I can use posso, puoi and polite può before an infinitive.

targets.label: Ask if you can do something
targets.explanation: Posso asks what I may do; puoi addresses a familiar person; può addresses one person politely as Lei.

repair.title: Try ask if you can do something again
repair.body: Potere: io posso, tu puoi, lui/lei/Lei può, noi possiamo, voi potete, loro possono. Follow it with the unchanged infinitive. Formal Lei uses può for a polite request.

examples.it: Possiamo aprire la porta? Voi potete leggere?
examples.en: May we open the door? Can you all read?

lessons.title: Say what you want or need to do
lessons.outcome: I can choose taught present forms of volere and dovere before a known infinitive.

targets.label: Say what you want or need to do
targets.explanation: Voglio + infinitive says what I want to do; devo + infinitive says what I need to do. Vuoi asks a familiar person about a wish.

repair.title: Try say what you want or need to do again
repair.body: Volere: io voglio, tu vuoi, lui/lei/Lei vuole, noi vogliamo, voi volete, loro vogliono. Dovere: io devo, tu devi, lui/lei/Lei deve, noi dobbiamo, voi dovete, loro devono. Follow either verb with the unchanged infinitive. In the reserve checks Anna vuole means Anna wants; Luca deve means Luca needs to or must.

examples.it: Anna vuole comprare il pane. Luca deve chiamare Anna.
examples.en: Anna wants to buy bread. Luca needs to call Anna.

examples.it: Noi vogliamo comprare un libro. Voi dovete chiamare Luca.
examples.en: We want to buy a book. You all need to call Luca.

lessons.title: Say what you like
lessons.outcome: I can choose mi piace or mi piacciono for a known thing.

targets.label: Say what you like
targets.explanation: Mi piace goes with one thing or an infinitive; mi piacciono goes with several things. The liked thing controls the verb.

repair.title: Try say what you like again
repair.body: Use mi piace before a singular thing or a verb in the infinitive.

examples.it: Mi piace la pizza. Mi piace leggere.
examples.en: I like pizza. I like reading.

lessons.title: Ask a familiar person to act
lessons.outcome: I can use a taught tu command and its negative.

targets.label: Ask a familiar person to act
targets.explanation: Parla, prendi and dormi are familiar tu commands. To tell someone not to act, use non + infinitive: non parlare.

repair.title: Try ask a familiar person to act again
repair.body: Speak to one familiar person: Parla, Prendi, Dormi.

examples.it: Prendi il libro, per favore.
examples.en: Take the book, please.

lessons.title: Join a simple reason
lessons.outcome: I can distinguish e, ma and perché in a short statement.

targets.label: Join a simple reason
targets.explanation: E adds a fact, ma contrasts one, and perché gives a reason. Choose the relation the speaker means.

repair.title: Try join a simple reason again
repair.body: Use e to add a compatible fact; use ma to contrast one.

examples.it: Ho un libro e uno zaino. Ho fame, ma non mangio.
examples.en: I have a book and a backpack. I am hungry, but I am not eating.

units.title: Describe a first completed event
units.description: Report a small completed event with taught auxiliaries and participles.

lessons.title: Say what you did yesterday
lessons.outcome: I can use avere plus a regular -ato participle for a completed act.

targets.label: Say what you did yesterday
targets.explanation: Ieri ho parlato and ieri ho mangiato describe finished events. Put a form of avere before the participle.

repair.title: Try say what you did yesterday again
repair.body: For these -are verbs, replace -are with -ato. Use ho, hai or ha before the participle.

examples.it: Ieri ho mangiato a casa. Anna ha comprato il pane.
examples.en: Yesterday I ate at home. Anna bought bread.

lessons.title: Finish another kind of verb
lessons.outcome: I can use the taught -uto and -ito participles with avere.

targets.label: Finish another kind of verb
targets.explanation: For selected regular verbs, ricevere → ricevuto and dormire → dormito. Learn the actual participle with its verb before using it.

repair.title: Try finish another kind of verb again
repair.body: Ricevere becomes ricevuto. Use the appropriate avere form first.

examples.it: Anna ha ricevuto un messaggio.
examples.en: Anna received a message.

lessons.title: Say you went or arrived
lessons.outcome: I can use selected essere past forms with stated subject agreement.

targets.label: Say you went or arrived
targets.explanation: Andare and arrivare take essere in these completed events. The participle matches the person: Anna è andata, Luca è arrivato.

repair.title: Try say you went or arrived again
repair.body: Use essere with andare: Luca è andato, Anna è andata.

examples.it: Luca è andato a Roma. Anna è andata a Milano.
examples.en: Luca went to Rome. Anna went to Milan.

lessons.title: Send a short note about yesterday
lessons.outcome: I can choose a taught completed form in a simple message.

targets.label: Send a short note about yesterday
targets.explanation: A message about a finished event uses a modeled passato prossimo form with the correct auxiliary and person; a time word helps but the finished meaning decides.

repair.title: Try send a short note about yesterday again
repair.body: Use one finished action you have learned, then say where or when it happened.

examples.it: Ieri ho comprato il pane. Anna è arrivata a Roma.
examples.en: Yesterday I bought bread. Anna arrived in Rome.

lessons.title: Use a short written message
lessons.outcome: I can find a practical detail in a short written message.

targets.label: I can find a practical detail in a short written message.
targets.explanation: A short message can give a destination, a time and a plan. Find the requested detail in the actual message.

repair.title: Find one detail at a time
repair.body: Return to the supported example, identify what the question asks for, then find that information in the message.

examples.it: Ciao, Anna! Domani vado a Roma. Parto alle nove. Luca
examples.en: Hi, Anna! Tomorrow I am going to Rome. I leave at nine. Luca

lessons.title: Understand a short spoken exchange
lessons.outcome: I can pick out a practical detail from a short recording.

targets.label: I can pick out a practical detail from a short recording.
targets.explanation: Listen for the requested item, number or time. Replaying is useful; reading the transcript makes this supported practice.

repair.title: Find one detail at a time
repair.body: Return to the supported example, identify what the question asks for, then find that information in the message.

examples.it: Vorrei un caffè, per favore. Costa due euro.
examples.en: I would like a coffee, please. It costs two euros.

units.title: Ask and answer
units.description: Open a question with the right word and give the answer it asks for.

lessons.title: Ask who, what, where and when
lessons.outcome: I can open a question with chi, che cosa, dove or quando and put the verb next.

targets.label: Ask who, what, where and when
targets.explanation: Chi asks about a person, che cosa (or cosa) about a thing, dove about a place and quando about a time. The question word comes first and the verb follows it: Dove abita Anna?

repair.title: Try ask who, what, where and when again
repair.body: Chi asks about a person, che cosa (or the short cosa) about a thing, dove about a place and quando about a time.

examples.it: Chi è? Che cosa mangi?
examples.en: Who is it? What are you eating?

lessons.title: Ask how, why, how many and which
lessons.outcome: I can ask with come, perché, quanto and quale, and make quanto and quale agree with the noun.

targets.label: Ask how, why, how many and which
targets.explanation: Come asks how and perché asks why. Before a noun, quanto agrees like an adjective: quanto pane, quanta acqua, quanti libri, quante case. Quale asks which and becomes quali in the plural.

repair.title: Try ask how, why, how many and which again
repair.body: Come asks how and perché asks why. Both come first, with the verb next.

examples.it: Come stai? Perché resti a casa?
examples.en: How are you? Why are you staying at home?

lessons.title: Match a question to its answer
lessons.outcome: I can give the kind of answer a question word asks for and use perché both for why and for because.

targets.label: Match a question to its answer
targets.explanation: The question word tells you what kind of answer to give: a person for chi, a place for dove, a time for quando, a reason for perché. Perché is why in the question and because in the answer.

repair.title: Try match a question to its answer again
repair.body: The question word tells you what kind of answer to give: a person for chi, a thing for che cosa, a place for dove, a time for quando.

examples.it: Dove abiti? Abito a Roma.
examples.en: Where do you live? I live in Rome.

units.title: Prepositions and articles
units.description: Join a and di to every article, including clock times and whose something is.

lessons.title: Join a to every article
lessons.outcome: I can choose al, allo, all’, alla, ai, agli or alle from the noun’s article, and say clock times.

targets.label: Join a to every article
targets.explanation: A joins the article of the noun: al mercato, allo stadio, all’ospedale, alla stazione, ai genitori, agli studenti, alle amiche. Clock hours take alle (alle otto), one o’clock takes all’una, and mezzogiorno and mezzanotte take a alone.

repair.title: Try join a to every article again
repair.body: A joins the article you already know: il → al, lo → allo, l’ → all’, la → alla.

examples.it: Vado al mercato. Anna è allo stadio. Luca è all’ospedale. Siamo alla stazione.
examples.en: I am going to the market. Anna is at the stadium. Luca is at the hospital. We are at the station.

lessons.title: Join di to every article
lessons.outcome: I can choose del, dello, dell’, della, dei, degli or delle to say whose something is or where it comes from.

targets.label: Join di to every article
targets.explanation: Di joins the article of the owner or the source: il libro del professore, la casa dello zio, il libro dell’amica, la casa della zia, i libri dei bambini, gli zaini degli studenti, il treno delle otto.

repair.title: Try join di to every article again
repair.body: Di joins the article of the owner or the source: il → del, lo → dello, l’ → dell’, la → della. Use the article of the owner, not of the thing owned.

examples.it: Il libro del professore. La casa dello zio. Il libro dell’amica. La casa della zia.
examples.en: The teacher’s book. The uncle’s house. The female friend’s book. The aunt’s house.

units.title: Describe a daily routine
units.description: Use a small reflexive pattern in ordinary routines.

lessons.title: Talk about my and your routine
lessons.outcome: I can use mi and ti with alzarsi.

targets.label: Talk about my and your routine
targets.explanation: Use mi alzo for me and ti alzi for familiar you. Keep the pronoun before the finite verb.

repair.title: Try talk about my and your routine again
repair.body: The subject and reflexive pronoun stay together.

examples.it: Io mi alzo presto.
examples.en: I get up early.

lessons.title: Describe someone else’s routine
lessons.outcome: I can use si or ci with alzarsi.

targets.label: Describe someone else’s routine
targets.explanation: Luca si alza, while noi ci alziamo. The pronoun and verb both change with the subject.

repair.title: Try describe someone else’s routine again
repair.body: A named singular person takes si alza.

examples.it: Luca si alza presto.
examples.en: Luca gets up early.

lessons.title: Describe washing in a routine
lessons.outcome: I can use mi lavo, ti lavi and si lava with a stated person.

targets.label: Describe washing in a routine
targets.explanation: Lavarsi follows the same present pattern as alzarsi: mi lavo, ti lavi, si lava.

repair.title: Try describe washing in a routine again
repair.body: The action returns to the speaker.

examples.it: Mi lavo prima di dormire.
examples.en: I wash before sleeping.

units.title: Report more completed events
units.description: Broaden familiar avere past forms through selected verbs.

lessons.title: Report a finished visit
lessons.outcome: I can use a modeled regular participle with avere.

targets.label: Report a finished visit
targets.explanation: A completed visit uses ho/hai/ha + visitato. The already learned ricevere and dormire use ricevuto and dormito.

repair.title: Try report a finished visit again
repair.body: Visitare has the regular participle visitato after avere.

examples.it: Ieri ho visitato il museo.
examples.en: Yesterday I visited the museum.

lessons.title: Use four common past forms
lessons.outcome: I can retrieve fatto, visto, preso and scritto.

targets.label: Use four common past forms
targets.explanation: Learn these participles with their verbs: fare → fatto, vedere → visto, prendere → preso, scrivere → scritto.

repair.title: Try use four common past forms again
repair.body: Fare → fatto, vedere → visto (also veduto), prendere → preso, scrivere → scritto. Learn the participle with its verb and retain valid alternatives.

examples.it: Ho fatto una torta. Ho visto Anna.
examples.en: I made a cake. I saw Anna.

examples.it: Ho veduto Anna. Ho preso il libro e ho scritto una lettera.
examples.en: I saw Anna. I took the book and wrote a letter.

lessons.title: Choose the person in the past
lessons.outcome: I can pair an avere auxiliary with a taught participle.

targets.label: Choose the person in the past
targets.explanation: The auxiliary carries person: ho, hai, ha, abbiamo, avete. With these verbs, the participle stays the same for the subject.

repair.title: Try choose the person in the past again
repair.body: Use ho for I, hai for familiar you, ha for a named singular person.

examples.it: Io ho visto Luca. Tu hai visto Anna?
examples.en: I saw Luca. Did you see Anna?

units.title: Describe travel and change
units.description: Use essere past forms, agreement, and reflexive completion.

lessons.title: Report a completed trip
lessons.outcome: I can use sono or sei with andato/andata.

targets.label: Report a completed trip
targets.explanation: Andare takes essere in the completed past. For a clearly stated singular person, -o describes a man and -a a woman.

repair.title: Try report a completed trip again
repair.body: A male speaker says sono andato; a female speaker says sono andata.

examples.it: Anna: «Sono andata a Roma.»
examples.en: Anna: “I went to Rome.”

lessons.title: Report where a group went
lessons.outcome: I can make plural participles agree after essere.

targets.label: Report where a group went
targets.explanation: A women-only group takes -e: sono andate. A men or mixed group takes -i: sono andati.

repair.title: Try report where a group went again
repair.body: Use -e for a group described as all women.

examples.it: Anna e Sara sono andate a Roma.
examples.en: Anna and Sara went to Rome.

lessons.title: Tell when you got up
lessons.outcome: I can use a modeled reflexive past with essere and agreement.

targets.label: Tell when you got up
targets.explanation: A completed reflexive action takes essere: mi sono alzato/alzata; Anna si è alzata. Match the ending to the person.

repair.title: Try tell when you got up again
repair.body: A male speaker says mi sono alzato; a female speaker says mi sono alzata.

examples.it: Anna: «Mi sono alzata presto.»
examples.en: Anna: “I got up early.”

lessons.title: Choose the auxiliary for a known verb
lessons.outcome: I can choose avere for a completed action or essere for known movement.

targets.label: Choose the auxiliary for a known verb
targets.explanation: Mangiare and comprare take avere here; andare and arrivare take essere here, with subject agreement.

repair.title: Try choose the auxiliary for a known verb again
repair.body: Avere introduces the taught eating and buying participles.

examples.it: Luca ha mangiato il pane.
examples.en: Luca ate the bread.

units.title: Set the scene in the past
units.description: Learn imperfect forms in descriptions and repeated past routines.

lessons.title: Describe a past routine
lessons.outcome: I can use parlavo and parlava for a past routine.

targets.label: Describe a past routine
targets.explanation: For a familiar -are verb, -avo describes what I used to do; -ava describes one other person.

repair.title: Try describe a past routine again
repair.body: Use parlavo for a repeated speaking habit in the past.

examples.it: Da piccolo parlavo italiano a casa.
examples.en: When I was little, I used to speak Italian at home.

lessons.title: Describe what someone used to do
lessons.outcome: I can use taught -ere/-ire imperfect forms in habitual contexts.

targets.label: Describe what someone used to do
targets.explanation: Leggere → leggevo/leggeva; dormire → dormivo/dormiva. These describe habitual or ongoing past activity.

repair.title: Try describe what someone used to do again
repair.body: Use leggevo for me, leggeva for a singular other person.

examples.it: Da piccolo leggevo ogni sera.
examples.en: As a boy, I used to read every evening.

lessons.title: Set a past scene
lessons.outcome: I can use ero, era, avevo and aveva for past states.

targets.label: Set a past scene
targets.explanation: The imperfect can set a scene or describe a state: ero/era for being, avevo/aveva for having.

repair.title: Try set a past scene again
repair.body: Ero and era describe an ongoing past state.

examples.it: Anna era stanca. Io ero a casa.
examples.en: Anna was tired. I was at home.

units.title: Tell a past story
units.description: Contrast the background with completed events in short narratives.

lessons.title: Distinguish habit from one event
lessons.outcome: I can choose imperfect for a habit and passato prossimo for one completed occasion.

targets.label: Distinguish habit from one event
targets.explanation: Ogni giorno calls for a repeated past routine; ieri once can frame a completed event. Meaning, not the time word alone, decides.

repair.title: Try distinguish habit from one event again
repair.body: Use imperfect for what happened regularly.

examples.it: Da piccolo parlavo italiano ogni giorno.
examples.en: As a boy, I spoke Italian every day.

lessons.title: Set a scene, then report an event
lessons.outcome: I can distinguish a background state from an event in a short story.

targets.label: Set a scene, then report an event
targets.explanation: Era and avevo set the scene. A completed act such as ha chiamato or è arrivata moves the story forward.

repair.title: Try set a scene, then report an event again
repair.body: Imperfect describes the state already in progress.

examples.it: Ero a casa e avevo fame.
examples.en: I was at home and hungry.

lessons.title: Retell a two-event afternoon
lessons.outcome: I can choose a background imperfect and two completed actions.

targets.label: Retell a two-event afternoon
targets.explanation: Keep the scene in imperfect and completed actions in passato prossimo. Do not convert every past verb to one tense.

repair.title: Try retell a two-event afternoon again
repair.body: Describe the place or condition before the action.

examples.it: Era una giornata calda.
examples.en: It was a warm day.

units.title: Show an action in progress
units.description: Use stare plus gerund only where ongoing viewpoint matters.

lessons.title: Say what is happening right now
lessons.outcome: I can use sto, stai or sta plus a taught gerund.

targets.label: Say what is happening right now
targets.explanation: Use stare plus -ando/-endo for an action in progress at this moment: sto parlando, Anna sta leggendo.

repair.title: Try say what is happening right now again
repair.body: Parlare becomes parlando after a form of stare.

examples.it: Sto parlando con Anna.
examples.en: I am speaking with Anna.

lessons.title: Choose a habit or an ongoing act
lessons.outcome: I can distinguish parlo from sto parlando by meaning.

targets.label: Choose a habit or an ongoing act
targets.explanation: Simple present can report a habit; stare + gerund highlights what is unfolding now. Both may be possible in some contexts; these prompts specify the intended meaning.

repair.title: Try choose a habit or an ongoing act again
repair.body: Use simple present for a regular habit.

examples.it: Parlo con Anna ogni giorno.
examples.en: I speak with Anna every day.

lessons.title: Describe an action underway then
lessons.outcome: I can use stavo or stava plus gerund for an ongoing past action.

targets.label: Describe an action underway then
targets.explanation: Stavo parlando sets an action in progress in the past. An event such as ha chiamato can interrupt it. Ordinary imperfetto may also describe an ongoing action; progressive adds explicit focus.

repair.title: Try describe an action underway then again
repair.body: Use stavo plus the gerund for me.

examples.it: Stavo parlando quando Anna ha chiamato.
examples.en: I was speaking when Anna called.

units.title: Keep track of people and things
units.description: Use direct objects after their referents are established.

lessons.title: Replace one known object
lessons.outcome: I can use lo or la for a clear singular object.

targets.label: Replace one known object
targets.explanation: Lo replaces a masculine singular direct object; la replaces a feminine singular one. Put it before a finite verb.

repair.title: Try replace one known object again
repair.body: Il libro is masculine: lo leggo.

examples.it: Il libro? Lo leggo oggi.
examples.en: The book? I am reading it today.

lessons.title: Replace several known objects
lessons.outcome: I can use li or le for a clear plural object.

targets.label: Replace several known objects
targets.explanation: Li replaces a masculine plural direct object; le replaces a feminine plural one. The referenced noun tells you which.

repair.title: Try replace several known objects again
repair.body: I libri become li when already known.

examples.it: I libri? Li leggo oggi.
examples.en: The books? I read them today.

lessons.title: Follow the object in a dialogue
lessons.outcome: I can choose a direct pronoun from its stated referent.

targets.label: Follow the object in a dialogue
targets.explanation: Before selecting lo, la, li or le, identify the object named in the previous line; grammatical gender and number belong to that noun.

repair.title: Try follow the object in a dialogue again
repair.body: The earlier noun controls the later pronoun.

examples.it: Anna: «Leggi il messaggio?» Luca: «Sì, lo leggo.»
examples.en: Anna: “Do you read the message?” Luca: “Yes, I read it.”

lessons.title: Say me, you, us and you all as objects
lessons.outcome: I can use mi, ti, ci and vi as direct objects before the verb.

targets.label: Say me, you, us and you all as objects
targets.explanation: Mi (me), ti (you), ci (us) and vi (you all) are direct objects that go before the verb, like lo and la: Mi vedi? Ti chiamo stasera. Ci aspetta. Vi invito.

repair.title: Try say me, you, us and you all as objects again
repair.body: Mi means me and ti means you as direct objects. They go before the verb, just like lo and la.

examples.it: Mi vedi? Ti chiamo stasera.
examples.en: Can you see me? I will call you this evening.

lessons.title: Shorten lo and la, and add non
lessons.outcome: I can write l’ before a verb that begins with a vowel and put non before the pronoun and verb.

targets.label: Shorten lo and la, and add non
targets.explanation: Before a vowel, lo and la shorten to l’ and join the verb: l’aspetto, l’ascolto. Non goes before the pronoun, never between the pronoun and the verb: Non lo so. Non la vedo.

repair.title: Try shorten lo and la, and add non again
repair.body: Before a vowel, lo/la can shorten to l’ and join the verb: l’aspetto, l’ascolto. Li/le do not shorten. Non goes before the clitic and verb: non lo so, non la vedo.

examples.it: Il treno? L’aspetto.
examples.en: The train? I am waiting for it.

examples.it: Il pane? Non lo compro.
examples.en: The bread? I am not buying it.

elision.title: Join the shortened clitic
elision.body: In the model lo/la shortens to l’ before a vowel and joins the verb: l’aspetto, l’ascolto. Li/le do not shorten.

examples.it: Il treno? L’aspetto. La radio? L’ascolto.
examples.en: The train? I am waiting for it. The radio? I listen to it.

non-first.title: Put non before the pronoun
non-first.body: Keep the order non + object pronoun + verb: non lo so, non la chiamo. Non cannot go between the pronoun and its verb.

examples.it: Il pane? Non lo compro. Sara? Non la chiamo.
examples.en: The bread? I am not buying it. Sara? I am not calling her.

lessons.title: Attach the pronoun to the verb
lessons.outcome: I can attach a direct pronoun to an infinitive after per or a modal, to a gerund and to a familiar command.

targets.label: Attach the pronoun to the verb
targets.explanation: After per the pronoun attaches to the infinitive, which drops its final -e: per vederlo. After a modal it can attach in the same way: posso chiamarti (it may also stay before the modal: ti posso chiamare). It also attaches to a gerund and to a tu command, written as one word: guardandola, guardalo!

repair.title: Try attach the pronoun to the verb again
repair.body: With an infinitive, the pronoun attaches to the end and the infinitive drops its final -e: per vederlo, posso chiamarti, voglio vederla. After per this is the only place for it; after a modal it may also stay before the modal (ti posso chiamare), a choice the next unit practises.

examples.it: Vado al cinema per vederlo. Posso chiamarti stasera?
examples.en: I am going to the cinema to see it. Can I call you this evening?

units.title: Give things to people
units.description: Distinguish recipients and choose a natural clitic position.

lessons.title: Name me or you as recipient
lessons.outcome: I can use mi or ti for a recipient with dare or scrivere.

targets.label: Name me or you as recipient
targets.explanation: Mi means to me and ti means to you in these modeled exchanges. Put the pronoun before the finite verb.

repair.title: Try name me or you as recipient again
repair.body: Use mi before the finite verb when I receive something.

examples.it: Anna mi scrive una lettera.
examples.en: Anna writes me a letter.

lessons.title: Choose the named recipient
lessons.outcome: I can use gli for a male recipient and le for a female recipient.

targets.label: Choose the named recipient
targets.explanation: Gli means to him; le means to her. The recipient receives something, while the direct object is the thing given.

repair.title: Try choose the named recipient again
repair.body: Luca receives a thing: gli do il libro.

examples.it: Luca? Gli do il libro.
examples.en: Luca? I give him the book.

lessons.title: Address our or your group as recipient
lessons.outcome: I can use ci and vi for group recipients in a clear exchange.

targets.label: Address our or your group as recipient
targets.explanation: Ci can mean to us and vi to you all when a person gives or writes something to that group. The thing given remains a separate direct object.

repair.title: Try address our or your group as recipient again
repair.body: Ci identifies we as the recipients.

examples.it: Anna ci scrive un messaggio.
examples.en: Anna writes us a message.

lessons.title: Keep a pronoun with a two-verb phrase
lessons.outcome: I can place a direct pronoun before a modal or attach it to an infinitive.

targets.label: Keep a pronoun with a two-verb phrase
targets.explanation: With posso vedere, both lo posso vedere and posso vederlo are standard. The attached form drops the infinitive’s final -e.

repair.title: Try keep a pronoun with a two-verb phrase again
repair.body: Place the object pronoun before the conjugated modal.

examples.it: Il libro? Lo posso vedere.
examples.en: The book? I can see it.

units.title: Plan ahead
units.description: Use modeled future forms for plans beyond the present.

lessons.title: Make a future plan
lessons.outcome: I can use parlerò, parlerai or parlerà for a future conversation.

targets.label: Make a future plan
targets.explanation: For this modeled -are verb, parl- takes future endings -erò, -erai, -erà. The subject tells which ending is needed.

repair.title: Try make a future plan again
repair.body: Io parlerò names a later conversation.

examples.it: Domani parlerò con Anna.
examples.en: Tomorrow I will speak with Anna.

lessons.title: Extend the regular future
lessons.outcome: I can use prenderò and dormirò for two later actions.

targets.label: Extend the regular future
targets.explanation: Prendere keeps prender- before future endings; dormire keeps dormir-. Learn these common forms in context.

repair.title: Try extend the regular future again
repair.body: Prenderò names a later act of taking.

examples.it: Domani prenderò il treno.
examples.en: Tomorrow I will take the train.

lessons.title: Use three common future stems
lessons.outcome: I can use sarò, avrò and andrò in a plan.

targets.label: Use three common future stems
targets.explanation: Essere, avere and andare have future stems sar-, avr-, and andr-. Learn the useful I forms and the modeled third-person forms.

repair.title: Try use three common future stems again
repair.body: Use sarò, avrò, andrò for my future state, possession or trip.

examples.it: Domani sarò a Roma.
examples.en: Tomorrow I will be in Rome.

lessons.title: Choose a present or future plan
lessons.outcome: I can use present for an arranged near plan and future for a later prediction or intention.

targets.label: Choose a present or future plan
targets.explanation: Italian often uses present for a scheduled near plan; future forms give an explicit future viewpoint. Prompts here specify the intended framing.

repair.title: Try choose a present or future plan again
repair.body: A stated near arrangement may use present.

examples.it: Stasera vado a casa di Anna.
examples.en: This evening I am going to Anna’s home.

units.title: Ask politely and imagine
units.description: Use small conditional chunks before broad hypothetical syntax.

lessons.title: Make a polite request
lessons.outcome: I can use vorrei, potrei and potrebbe in a polite exchange.

targets.label: Make a polite request
targets.explanation: Vorrei asks for a desired thing; potrei asks whether I may; potrebbe addresses someone politely about their ability or willingness.

repair.title: Try make a polite request again
repair.body: Vorrei is a polite request for something.

examples.it: Vorrei un caffè, per favore.
examples.en: I would like a coffee, please.

lessons.title: Say what I would do
lessons.outcome: I can use vorrei, andrei and farei for a tentative plan.

targets.label: Say what I would do
targets.explanation: Conditional forms can make a wish or tentative idea less direct: vorrei visitare, andrei, farei.

repair.title: Try say what i would do again
repair.body: Vorrei plus infinitive expresses a polite wish.

examples.it: Vorrei visitare Roma.
examples.en: I would like to visit Rome.

lessons.title: Address Lei politely
lessons.outcome: I can distinguish familiar puoi from polite potrebbe in a real request.

targets.label: Address Lei politely
targets.explanation: Use familiar puoi with a peer; polite potrebbe with Lei or a stranger. The conditional softens a request without changing who acts.

repair.title: Try address lei politely again
repair.body: A familiar peer can receive puoi plus infinitive.

examples.it: Luca, puoi aiutarmi?
examples.en: Luca, can you help me?

steps.title: Ask a stranger and a friend

units.title: Compare and measure
units.description: Make bounded comparisons and describe quantities.

lessons.title: Compare two things
lessons.outcome: I can use più or meno with di for two compared nouns or people.

targets.label: Compare two things
targets.explanation: Più/meno + adjective + di compares two nouns or people. The adjective still agrees with what is described.

repair.title: Try compare two things again
repair.body: Luca is the person described; più alto di compares him with Marco.

examples.it: Luca è più alto di Marco.
examples.en: Luca is taller than Marco.

lessons.title: Compare two actions
lessons.outcome: I can use più or meno with che when comparing two activities.

targets.label: Compare two actions
targets.explanation: When one person does one action more or less than another action, use più/meno ... che between the actions.

repair.title: Try compare two actions again
repair.body: Compare leggere with scrivere for the same person.

examples.it: Leggo più che scrivo.
examples.en: I read more than I write.

lessons.title: Identify the tallest in a known group
lessons.outcome: I can use il più or la più with a defined group.

targets.label: Identify the tallest in a known group
targets.explanation: A relative superlative identifies the highest degree within a stated group: il più alto, la più alta. Keep article and adjective agreement.

repair.title: Try identify the tallest in a known group again
repair.body: Il più alto refers to a man compared with his group.

examples.it: Luca è il più alto del gruppo.
examples.en: Luca is the tallest in the group.

lessons.title: Emphasize a very strong quality
lessons.outcome: I can use -issimo/-issima with a taught adjective.

targets.label: Emphasize a very strong quality
targets.explanation: Bellissimo and bellissima express a very high degree without comparing a group. The ending agrees with the described noun.

repair.title: Try emphasize a very strong quality again
repair.body: Il libro is masculine: bellissimo or grandissimo.

examples.it: Il libro è bellissimo.
examples.en: The book is very beautiful.

lessons.title: Choose a useful quantity
lessons.outcome: I can distinguish qualche, alcuni and un po’ di in familiar shopping contexts.

targets.label: Choose a useful quantity
targets.explanation: Qualche takes a singular noun but means a few; alcuni takes a masculine plural noun; un po’ di can precede a mass noun.

repair.title: Try choose a useful quantity again
repair.body: After qualche, the noun stays singular.

examples.it: Compro qualche libro.
examples.en: I buy a few books.

units.title: Give clear instructions
units.description: Distinguish familiar commands from polite Lei commands.

lessons.title: Give a familiar instruction
lessons.outcome: I can use familiar tu commands for taught verbs.

targets.label: Give a familiar instruction
targets.explanation: For the modeled verbs, parla, prendi and dormi address one familiar person. A positive command does not include tu.

repair.title: Try give a familiar instruction again
repair.body: Parla or aspetta addresses a familiar person.

examples.it: Luca, parla più piano.
examples.en: Luca, speak more slowly.

lessons.title: Address more than one person
lessons.outcome: I can use voi commands with familiar verbs.

targets.label: Address more than one person
targets.explanation: For the taught verbs, plural-you commands are parlate, prendete and dormite. Put non before the same plural command to prohibit an action.

repair.title: Try address more than one person again
repair.body: Use parlate or prendete with more than one addressee.

examples.it: Anna e Luca, parlate piano.
examples.en: Anna and Luca, speak quietly.

lessons.title: Give a polite instruction
lessons.outcome: I can use formal Lei commands for taught verbs.

targets.label: Give a polite instruction
targets.explanation: Formal Lei uses parli, prenda, aspetti in these modeled instructions. Address the listener politely; do not switch to familiar tu forms.

repair.title: Try give a polite instruction again
repair.body: Parli addresses one person formally.

examples.it: Signora, parli più piano, per favore.
examples.en: Madam, speak more slowly, please.

lessons.title: Tell someone not to act
lessons.outcome: I can form a negative familiar or polite instruction.

targets.label: Tell someone not to act
targets.explanation: Negative tu uses non + infinitive: non parlare. Negative formal Lei uses non + polite command: non parli.

repair.title: Try tell someone not to act again
repair.body: Use non plus the infinitive with familiar tu.

examples.it: Luca, non parlare adesso.
examples.en: Luca, do not speak now.

units.title: Locate and measure time
units.description: Choose da and common contracted prepositions in bounded contexts.

lessons.title: Say where someone comes from
lessons.outcome: I can use da with venire for a named place.

targets.label: Say where someone comes from
targets.explanation: Vengo da Roma names origin or departure. In this lesson the place is a city and needs no article.

repair.title: Try say where someone comes from again
repair.body: Use vengo da before a city.

examples.it: Vengo da Roma.
examples.en: I come from Rome.

lessons.title: Say how long a state has lasted
lessons.outcome: I can use da with present for a state continuing up to now.

targets.label: Say how long a state has lasted
targets.explanation: Abito qui da due anni means I have lived here for two years and still live here. Italian uses present in this ongoing frame.

repair.title: Try say how long a state has lasted again
repair.body: Present plus da names duration up to now.

examples.it: Abito qui da due anni.
examples.en: I have lived here for two years.

lessons.title: Read source and possession contractions
lessons.outcome: I can understand del and dal with masculine singular nouns.

targets.label: Read source and possession contractions
targets.explanation: Di + il becomes del in a relation such as the book of the teacher; da + il becomes dal for from the person or place.

repair.title: Try read source and possession contractions again
repair.body: Del joins di and il before a masculine noun.

examples.it: Il libro del professore è qui.
examples.en: The teacher’s book is here.

lessons.title: Use common place contractions
lessons.outcome: I can use al, nel and sul with familiar place nouns.

targets.label: Use common place contractions
targets.explanation: A + il becomes al; in + il becomes nel; su + il becomes sul. Learn each with its place meaning.

repair.title: Try use common place contractions again
repair.body: Vado al museo; sono nel museo.

examples.it: Vado al museo. Sono nel museo.
examples.en: I go to the museum. I am in the museum.

lessons.title: Join in, su and da to every article
lessons.outcome: I can choose the right form of in, su and da with any article.

targets.label: Join in, su and da to every article
targets.explanation: In, su and da join the article like a and di: nel, nello, nell’, nella, nei, negli, nelle; sul, sullo, sull’, sulla, sui, sugli, sulle; dal, dallo, dall’, dalla, dai, dagli, dalle. Choose the preposition from the meaning, then the form from the noun’s article.

repair.title: Try join in, su and da to every article again
repair.body: In, su and da join the article exactly like a and di. Singular: nel, nello, nell’, nella; sul, sullo, sull’, sulla; dal, dallo, dall’, dalla.

examples.it: Il libro è nello zaino. La chiave è sulla sedia. Vengo dall’ufficio.
examples.en: The book is in the backpack. The key is on the chair. I am coming from the office.

units.title: Connect and understand a small story
units.description: Link causes, referents, and real possibilities.

lessons.title: Link a reason and sequence
lessons.outcome: I can use perché, poi and quindi for different relations.

targets.label: Link a reason and sequence
targets.explanation: Perché gives a reason; poi marks what happens next; quindi introduces a consequence. Context decides which relation is intended.

repair.title: Try link a reason and sequence again
repair.body: Give the reason after perché.

examples.it: Resto a casa perché piove.
examples.en: I stay home because it is raining.

lessons.title: Identify a thing with che
lessons.outcome: I can join two short ideas with relative che.

targets.label: Identify a thing with che
targets.explanation: Relative che means who or that in these short clauses and does not change form for person, gender or number.

repair.title: Try identify a thing with che again
repair.body: The second clause identifies the already named noun.

examples.it: Il libro che leggo è piccolo.
examples.en: The book that I am reading is small.

lessons.title: Talk about a real possibility
lessons.outcome: I can use se with present for an open real condition.

targets.label: Talk about a real possibility
targets.explanation: Se plus present can state a real possibility; the other clause can use present or a learned future form. This lesson does not teach hypothetical se + subjunctive.

repair.title: Try talk about a real possibility again
repair.body: Se piove, resto a casa describes what I do if rain happens.

examples.it: Se piove, resto a casa.
examples.en: If it rains, I stay home.

lessons.title: Read a short past story
lessons.outcome: I can find who did what in a short past narrative.

targets.label: Read a short past story
targets.explanation: I can find who did what in a short past narrative.

repair.title: Find the detail again
repair.body: First locate the completed action in the short story.

examples.it: Anna era a casa. Luca ha chiamato.
examples.en: Anna was at home. Luca called.

lessons.title: Understand a short spoken request
lessons.outcome: I can identify the request or answer in a new service exchange.

targets.label: Understand a short spoken request
targets.explanation: I can identify the request or answer in a new service exchange.

repair.title: Find the detail again
repair.body: A speaker may ask for an item using vorrei.

examples.it: Vorrei un biglietto, per favore.
examples.en: I would like a ticket, please.

units.title: Someone, something, somewhere
units.description: Talk about unnamed people, things and places, say that there is nobody or nothing, and link replies naturally.

lessons.title: Talk about someone, something and somewhere
lessons.outcome: I can use qualcuno for an unnamed person, qualcosa for an unnamed thing, qualche with a singular noun and da qualche parte for an unknown place.

targets.label: Talk about someone, something and somewhere
targets.explanation: Qualcuno is someone and qualcosa is something: both are singular and take a singular verb; qualcosa never changes, and qualcuno becomes qualcuna only when the person is clearly a woman. Qualche means some or a few and always takes a singular noun: qualche minuto. Da qualche parte means somewhere.

repair.title: Try talk about someone, something and somewhere again
repair.body: Qualcuno names a person you do not identify; qualcosa names a thing. Both are singular, so the verb is singular too. Qualcosa never changes; qualcuno becomes qualcuna only when the person is clearly a woman.

examples.it: C’è qualcuno alla porta. Vuoi qualcosa da bere?
examples.en: There is someone at the door. Do you want something to drink?

lessons.title: Say nobody and nothing
lessons.outcome: I can use nessuno and niente with non after the verb, and without non when they open the sentence.

targets.label: Say nobody and nothing
targets.explanation: After the verb, nessuno and niente need non before the verb: Non vedo nessuno. Non mangio niente. When nessuno or niente opens the sentence, non disappears: Nessuno risponde. Niente è pronto. Nulla means the same as niente.

repair.title: Try say nobody and nothing again
repair.body: When nessuno or niente follows the verb, non still goes before the verb. The two words make one negative, not two.

examples.it: Non vedo nessuno. Non mangio niente.
examples.en: I see nobody. I eat nothing.

lessons.title: Link replies with everyday words
lessons.outcome: I can choose allora or dunque to draw a conclusion, però or invece to contrast, and anche or infatti to add or confirm.

targets.label: Link replies with everyday words
targets.explanation: Allora and dunque draw a conclusion: so, then. Però contrasts like ma and can sit inside the reply; invece sets one person or thing against another: instead, on the other hand. Anche adds too, right before the word it adds; infatti confirms what was just said: in fact.

repair.title: Try link replies with everyday words again
repair.body: Allora and dunque mean so or then: what follows is the result of the situation. Allora is the everyday word; dunque is a little more formal.

examples.it: Piove. Allora resto a casa.
examples.en: It is raining. So I stay at home.

units.title: Tell what happened
units.description: Build a connected account with scene, event, sequence and outcome.

lessons.title: An event in progress
lessons.outcome: I can say what was happening when one event occurred.

targets.label: Place a background action and an event on one timeline
targets.explanation: The imperfetto presents an action already underway; the passato prossimo marks the event that happened during it.

repair.title: Which action was already underway?
repair.body: Locate the action in progress first. Put that scene in the imperfetto; put the new bounded event in the passato prossimo.

examples.it: Leggevo quando è arrivata Sara.
examples.en: I was reading when Sara arrived.

lessons.title: Move a story forward
lessons.outcome: I can recount a short sequence with clear time markers.

targets.label: Move a story forward
targets.explanation: First locate the account in time; use a completed form for the first event. Poi moves the listener to another event; alla fine gives the outcome.

repair.title: Try move a story forward again
repair.body: First locate the account in time; use a completed form for the first event. Poi moves the listener to another event; alla fine gives the outcome.

examples.it: Ieri ho preso l’autobus alle otto.
examples.en: Yesterday I took the bus at eight.

lessons.title: Explain the outcome
lessons.outcome: I can connect an unexpected event to what happened next.

targets.label: Explain the outcome
targets.explanation: Tell the listener what happened before giving the result. Per questo introduces the practical consequence.

repair.title: Try explain the outcome again
repair.body: Tell the listener what happened before giving the result. Per questo introduces the practical consequence.

examples.it: Ho perso l’autobus.
examples.en: I missed the bus.

units.title: Explain what happened earlier
